narrative:
The model estimates a 49% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

The decision was driven mainly by three key factors. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence and pulled the prediction toward staying. Most employees the model expects to stay have similar short experience of 1-5 years, so the system sees you as typical of loyal, early-career staff. Second, not having received other job offers while working here also pushed the prediction toward staying; the majority of employees predicted to remain likewise report no external opportunities.

However, one factor worked against you. Your difficult work-life balance was the most important reason the model still leaned toward leaving. Only 9% of employees the system expects to stay report a difficult balance, so the model interpreted this as a clear warning sign that you may eventually look for a change.

The company should discuss your work-life balance with you openly and explore adjustments such as flexible hours or reduced overtime. At the same time, you may want to reflect on whether small changes in your current role could improve that balance enough for you to stay and grow here. Addressing this area could shift the outlook in future reviews.
